interactions.summary: Jiang pushes the class to compare meritocracy with older nobility, and students answer that meritocracy at least claims to value skill while still being heavily shaped by family advantage and the birth lottery.

Jiang answers that meritocracy legitimates inequality because winners think they deserve their position, then maps Dante's cruelty in Florence onto modern competitive cruelty among classmates and elites.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang lecture monologue with brief student interjection

interactions.summary: A student reads the next Inferno passage in which Farinata asks why Florence remains so cruel to his kin.

speaker_notes.note: The student cites social-science and higher-education critique to argue that meritocracy is an incomplete upgrade over aristocracy rather than a clean break from it.
The short student phrase is an interpretive gloss on Jiang's point, not a standalone public question.

claims.claim: Jiang says elite universities with many legacies already look like an aristocracy or oligarchy rather than a pure meritocracy.
A student argues that meritocracy differs from aristocracy because it officially values education, talent, critical thinking, and problem-solving rather than birth alone.

A student says contemporary meritocracy remains shaped by aristocratic inheritance because socioeconomic status strongly shapes academic outcomes, even when people believe they earned everything through hard work.
Jiang argues that meritocracy intensifies inequality because people at the top believe the system is fair and that they deserved their advantages.
Jiang says meritocracy often rewards credentials rather than actual skill or talent.
Jiang links the ruthless competition of Florence in Dante to modern competitive behavior such as hiding a classmate's admission letter, arguing that rivalry turns even friends into enemies.
Jiang reads Cavalcante's question about his son as proof of paternal love and says Dante's implied answer punishes the father a second time.

signature_moments.moment: Meritocracy becomes more dangerous than old nobility because winners think inequality is deserved rather than embarrassing.
signature_moments.source_phrase: people who've been from meritocracy think they deserved it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens Jiang's argument that ideology can intensify hierarchy by moralizing privilege.

signature_moments.moment: Competitive society makes friends see each other as enemies.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This line bridges Dante's civic cruelty with Jiang's running critique of modern competitive order.

signature_moments.moment: Dante's cruelty is framed as killing a father twice.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the packet's moral charge into one memorable image of competitive punishment beyond death.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Used to name the inherited family and class advantages that make meritocracy less earned than it appears.
Jiang contrasts credentials with real skill to argue that meritocratic systems often reward institutional markers rather than ability.

chronology_notes.note: This packet closes the meritocracy detour by using it to illuminate cruelty in Dante's Florence, then returns to close reading with Farinata's question.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's empirical formulation about socioeconomic status and academic performance is noisy in ASR and is preserved as an in-class claim rather than a verified statistic.
